title: Ἡ τοῦ μεγάρου κάθαρσις
titleEn: The Cleansing of the Hall — Odyssey 22.398–501
about: Eurycleia opens the doors and Telemachus leads her to Odysseus, who stands among the dead spattered with blood like a lion fresh from its kill. She is ready to cry out in triumph, but he stops her, says that it is not right to boast over slain men, and asks which of the women have dishonoured him. She answers that twelve of the fifty maidservants have shamed the house, and Odysseus tells Telemachus and the two herdsmen to carry out the corpses, have the women wash the hall, and then lead them out and kill them. Telemachus instead hangs them in a row from a ship's cable, like birds caught in a snare, and Melanthius is dragged out and mutilated. The men wash and come back, and Odysseus has the nurse bring sulphur and fire to purify the hall and call the women. They come with torches, throw their arms round him and kiss him, and he is seized by a longing to weep.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρ’ ἐφώνησεν, τῇ δ’ ἄπτερος ἔπλετο μῦθος,
ὤϊξεν δὲ θύρας μεγάρων εὖ ναιεταόντων,
βῆ δ’ ἴμεν·
sentences.i: So he spoke, and for her the speech was wingless; she opened the doors of the well-inhabited halls and set out;
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph. The first line is a line already published, and keeps its English. Telemachus, who has just called the nurse, is the one who spoke. τῇ δ’ ἄπτερος ἔπλετο μῦθος turns the formula ἔπεα πτερόεντα 'winged words' inside out, 'to her the speech was wingless'; it may mean that she made no reply, but the Greek does not say so. ἔπλετο is an aorist of πέλομαι 'come to be', and it carries the ordinary augment. ὤϊξεν is a past tense of οἴγνυμι 'open'; its subject, the nurse, is not named. ναιεταόντων is the uncontracted participle of ναιετάω 'dwell'. βῆ δ’ ἴμεν is 'set out to go': βῆ is the unaugmented aorist of βαίνω and ἴμεν the infinitive (Attic ἰέναι). The ano teleia closes the unit in mid-line.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ Τηλέμαχος πρόσθ’ ἡγεμόνευεν.
sentences.l: but Telemachus before led the way.
sentences.i: while Telemachus went in front, leading the way.
sentences.n: αὐτάρ is 'but, and'; the nurse goes, and Telemachus goes before her. πρόσθ’ is πρόσθε 'in front', elided, and ἡγεμόνευεν is the imperfect of ἡγεμονεύω 'act as leader, guide', the verb of ἡγεμών 'leader'. The Greek gives no more of the walk than this: the next line is the nurse's discovery.

sentences.t:
εὗρεν ἔπειτ’ Ὀδυσῆα μετὰ κταμένοισι νέκυσσιν,
αἵματι καὶ λύθρῳ πεπαλαγμένον ὥστε λέοντα,
ὅς ῥά τε βεβρωκὼς βοὸς ἔρχεται ἀγραύλοιο·
sentences.i: Then she found Odysseus among the slain corpses, spattered with blood and gore, like a lion that comes along after eating a field-dwelling ox;
sentences.n: εὗρεν is the unaugmented aorist of εὑρίσκω 'find'; the subject is the nurse, again unnamed. κταμένοισι is the dative plural of a short-form aorist participle of κτείνω, 'slain', and νέκυσσιν the dative plural of νέκυς 'corpse', with -σσι for Attic -σι. πεπαλαγμένον is the perfect passive participle of παλάσσω 'spatter, besmear', agreeing with Ὀδυσῆα, and λύθρος is gore, blood that defiles. ὥστε begins a simile. In ὅς ῥά τε βεβρωκὼς ... ἔρχεται the epic particles ῥά τε mark a general picture, true of lions as a kind; βεβρωκώς is the perfect participle of βιβρώσκω 'eat', governing the genitive βοός, and ἀγραύλοιο, a genitive in -οιο, is 'field-dwelling', from ἀγρός 'field' and αὐλή: an ox that lives out of doors.

sentences.t:
πᾶν δ’ ἄρα οἱ στῆθός τε παρήϊά τ’ ἀμφοτέρωθεν
αἱματόεντα πέλει, δεινὸς δ’ εἰς ὦπα ἰδέσθαι·
sentences.l:
and all his chest and his cheeks on both sides
are bloody, and he is dread to look upon in the face;
sentences.i: his whole chest and both his cheeks are bloody, and he is dread to look at in the face;
sentences.n: The simile goes on. οἱ is the dative 'his', a dative of the possessor, and refers to the lion. παρήϊα is the plural of παρήϊον 'cheek', ἀμφοτέρωθεν 'on both sides' has the suffix -θεν, and αἱματόεντα is built on αἷμα 'blood' with -όεις 'full of'. πέλει is 'is', the present of πέλω. δεινός 'dread' is the house rendering, here 'fearful'. εἰς ὦπα ἰδέσθαι is 'to look at in the face': ὤψ (accusative ὦπα) is 'face, look', and ἰδέσθαι an aorist infinitive of respect, 'dread as to the sight'.

sentences.t: ὣς Ὀδυσεὺς πεπάλακτο πόδας καὶ χεῖρας ὕπερθεν.
sentences.l: So Odysseus was spattered on feet and hands above.
sentences.i: So Odysseus was spattered, on his feet and on his hands above.
sentences.n: ὣς answers the ὥστε of the simile: 'so'. πεπάλακτο is the pluperfect passive of παλάσσω, the finite form of the participle at 402, with no augment: 'was spattered'. πόδας καὶ χεῖρας are accusatives of respect, 'in feet and hands'. ὕπερθεν 'above' is left as it stands: whether it means the upper side of the feet and hands, or something wider, the Greek does not say.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ ὡς οὖν νέκυάς τε καὶ ἄσπετον εἴσιδεν αἷμα,
ἴθυσέν ῥ’ ὀλολύξαι, ἐπεὶ μέγα εἴσιδεν ἔργον·
sentences.l:
And she, when then the corpses and the boundless blood she saw,
was eager to raise the ritual cry, since a great deed she saw;
sentences.i: And when she saw the corpses and the boundless blood, she was eager to raise the ritual cry, for she saw a great deed;
sentences.n: ἡ is the old 'article' used as a pronoun, 'she', and ὡς unaccented is 'when'. νέκυάς is the accusative plural of νέκυς. ἄσπετος is 'boundless', literally 'not to be told', used of what is too much to be put in words. εἴσιδεν is the unaugmented aorist of εἰσοράω 'look upon', and it comes again in the second line. ἴθυσε (with ῥ’ for the particle ῥα) is the aorist of ἰθύω 'go straight at, be eager'. ὀλολύξαι is the aorist infinitive of ὀλολύζω, the loud ritual cry that women raised at a sacrifice and at a victory: Odysseus holds her back from it in the next unit. ἔργον is 'deed, piece of work'; the same word returns at 479, 'the work was finished'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ Ὀδυσεὺς κατέρυκε καὶ ἔσχεθεν ἱεμένην περ,
καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
but Odysseus held her back and restrained her, eager though she was,
and, lifting his voice, to her winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: but Odysseus held her back and checked her, eager as she was, and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to her:
sentences.n: The second line is a line already published, and keeps its English. κατέρυκε is the imperfect of κατερύκω 'hold back', and ἔσχεθεν a longer aorist form of ἔχω, 'held in check'. ἱεμένην is the middle participle of ἵημι 'be eager', feminine to match the nurse, and περ gives it concessive force, 'eager though she was'. καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is a speech formula: φωνήσας 'lifting his voice', and ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα 'spoke winged words', the house rendering. The ano teleia introduces the speech.

sentences.t: ἐν θυμῷ, γρηῦ, χαῖρε καὶ ἴσχεο μηδ’ ὀλόλυζε·
sentences.l: “In your heart, old woman, rejoice, and hold yourself back, and do not raise the ritual cry;
sentences.i: “Rejoice in your heart, old woman, but hold yourself back and do not raise the ritual cry;
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph. Odysseus speaks. ἐν θυμῷ 'in your heart' stands first for emphasis: let the joy stay inward. γρηῦ is the vocative of γρηῦς 'old woman'. χαῖρε here is the plain imperative of χαίρω 'rejoice', not the greeting 'welcome'. ἴσχεο is the middle imperative of ἴσχω 'hold in check', with -εο for Attic -ου. μηδ’ ὀλόλυζε is a prohibition with the present imperative, 'and do not go on crying out', and the verb is the one she was about to use in the unit before.

sentences.t: οὐχ ὁσίη κταμένοισιν ἐπ’ ἀνδράσιν εὐχετάασθαι.
sentences.l: Not holy it is, over slain men, to boast.
sentences.i: It is not right to boast over slain men.
sentences.n: The verb 'is' is left out: οὐχ ὁσίη (ἐστί). ὁσίη is what the gods allow, what is right in their sight. κταμένοισιν ἐπ’ ἀνδράσιν is 'over slain men', the dative with ἐπί, and εὐχετάασθαι is the uncontracted infinitive of εὐχετάομαι 'boast' (Attic εὐχετᾶσθαι). The cry of triumph is the boast he means.

sentences.t: τούσδε δὲ μοῖρ’ ἐδάμασσε θεῶν καὶ σχέτλια ἔργα·
sentences.l: These the fate of the gods subdued, and their cruel deeds;
sentences.i: These men the fate from the gods overcame, and their own cruel deeds;
sentences.n: τούσδε 'these' points at the dead. μοῖρ’ is μοῖρα 'portion, fate', with θεῶν 'of the gods' attached to it, so a fate that comes from the gods. ἐδάμασσε is the aorist of δαμάζω 'subdue, overcome', and it has two subjects: the fate and the deeds. σχέτλιος is 'cruel', one who does not shrink from anything.

sentences.t:
οὔ τινα γὰρ τίεσκον ἐπιχθονίων ἀνθρώπων,
οὐ κακὸν οὐδὲ μὲν ἐσθλόν, ὅτις σφέας εἰσαφίκοιτο·
sentences.l:
for none they honoured of men upon the earth,
not base and not good, whoever came to them;
sentences.i: for they honoured no one of the men who live on the earth, neither base nor good, whoever came to them;
sentences.n: τίεσκον is an imperfect with the iterative suffix -σκ-, from τίω 'honour': 'they never honoured', as a habit. ἐπιχθονίων ἀνθρώπων is 'men upon the earth', ἐπιχθόνιος being built on χθών 'earth'. οὐ κακὸν οὐδὲ μὲν ἐσθλόν puts masculine adjectives in apposition to οὔ τινα, 'not a base man, not a good one'; κακός is 'base' and ἐσθλός 'good'. ὅτις with the optative εἰσαφίκοιτο (εἰς + ἀφικνέομαι) is 'whoever came to them', an indefinite clause of repeated past action. σφέας is the accusative plural 'them'.

sentences.t: τῷ καὶ ἀτασθαλίῃσιν ἀεικέα πότμον ἐπέσπον.
sentences.l: Therefore too, by their wanton-follies, an unseemly doom they met.
sentences.i: That is why, through their wanton folly, they met an unseemly doom.
sentences.n: This line is already published, and keeps its English. τῷ is an old dative of the pronoun used as an adverb, 'therefore, for that reason'. ἀτασθαλίῃσιν is a dative plural in -ῃσιν, and ἐπέσπον the aorist of ἐφέπω 'meet, follow up'. ἀεικέα is the accusative singular of ἀεικής 'unseemly', agreeing with πότμον 'doom'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε μοι σὺ γυναῖκας ἐνὶ μεγάροις κατάλεξον,
αἵ τέ μ’ ἀτιμάζουσι καὶ αἳ νηλείτιδές εἰσιν.
sentences.l:
But come, you, to me the women in the halls recount,
both those who dishonour me and those who guiltless are.”
sentences.i: But come, you, give me an account of the women in the halls, both those who dishonour me and those who are guiltless.”
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε is 'but come', and σύ 'you' turns to the nurse as the one who knows. κατάλεξον is the aorist imperative of καταλέγω 'recount in order'; the verb comes again in her answer. αἵ τέ ... καὶ αἳ is 'both those who ... and those who': both are the relative pronoun, the first with epic τε. ἀτιμάζουσι is 'treat without honour, dishonour'. νηλείτιδες 'guiltless' is a rare word, and 'guiltless' is the traditional gloss. This ends the speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε φίλη τροφὸς Εὐρύκλεια·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed the dear nurse Eurycleia:
sentences.i: Then his dear nurse Eurycleia spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph. This line is already published, and keeps its English. It is the formula for a speaker who replies in turn: τὸν is 'him' (a pronoun), αὖτε 'in turn', προσέειπε 'addressed', and φίλη τροφός Εὐρύκλεια is the standing description of the nurse.

sentences.t: τοιγὰρ ἐγώ τοι, τέκνον, ἀληθείην καταλέξω.
sentences.l: “Well then, I to you, child, the truth will recount.
sentences.i: “Well then, my child, I will tell you the truth.
sentences.n: Eurycleia speaks. This line is already published, and keeps its English. τοιγάρ is 'well then, accordingly'. τοι is σοι 'to you', and τέκνον 'child' is her address to Odysseus. ἀληθείην is the Ionic accusative of ἀλήθεια 'the truth'. καταλέξω is the future (or a short-vowel subjunctive) of the verb he used in his command: she will recount them as he asked.

sentences.t:
πεντήκοντά τοί εἰσιν ἐνὶ μεγάροισι γυναῖκες
δμῳαί, τὰς μέν τ’ ἔργα διδάξαμεν ἐργάζεσθαι,
εἴριά τε ξαίνειν καὶ δουλοσύνην ἀνέχεσθαι·
sentences.i: There are fifty women in the halls, maids, whom we taught to do their tasks, to card wool and to bear slavery;
sentences.n: πεντήκοντα is 'fifty', and τοί here is the particle 'indeed, mark you', not the pronoun 'to you' of the line before. δμῳαί are 'maidservants'. τὰς μέν τ’ is 'those whom': τάς is the pronoun used as a relative, with epic τε. διδάξαμεν is the aorist of διδάσκω, and the 'we' is the household. ἔργα ἐργάζεσθαι is 'to do their tasks', the root repeated: 'to work work'. εἴρια is 'wool' (Attic ἔρια), ξαίνειν 'to card' it, and δουλοσύνη 'slavery' states the status plainly; ἀνέχεσθαι is 'to bear, endure'.

sentences.t:
τάων δώδεκα πᾶσαι ἀναιδείης ἐπέβησαν,
οὔτ’ ἐμὲ τίουσαι οὔτ’ αὐτὴν Πηνελόπειαν.
sentences.l:
Of these twelve in all have set foot on shamelessness,
honouring neither me nor Penelope herself.
sentences.i: Twelve of them in all have taken to shamelessness, honouring neither me nor Penelope herself.
sentences.n: τάων is the genitive plural of the pronoun, 'of those', partitive, with δώδεκα πᾶσαι 'twelve, all of them'. ἐπέβησαν is the aorist of ἐπιβαίνω 'set foot on, enter upon', governing ἀναιδείης, the Ionic genitive of ἀναίδεια 'shamelessness', built on ἀ- and αἰδώς 'respect'. οὔτ’ ... οὔτ’ is 'neither ... nor', and τίουσαι the participle of τίω 'honour' (the verb of τίεσκον above). Penelope has no epithet here.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχος δὲ νέον μὲν ἀέξετο, οὐδέ ἑ μήτηρ
σημαίνειν εἴασκεν ἐπὶ δμῳῇσι γυναιξίν.
sentences.l:
But Telemachus only lately was growing up, nor him his mother
would let give orders over the maidservant women.
sentences.i: But Telemachus was only just growing up, and his mother would not let him give orders to the maids.
sentences.n: ἀέξετο is the imperfect middle of ἀέξω 'grow, increase' (Attic αὐξάνω), and νέον is 'newly, lately'. ἑ is the pronoun 'him', accusative. εἴασκεν is an iterative imperfect of ἐάω 'allow', with the -σκ- suffix again: 'would never allow'. σημαίνειν, 'to give a sign', means here 'to give orders', and ἐπὶ δμῳῇσι γυναιξίν is 'over the maidservant women', with δμῳῇσι the dative plural in -ῃσι of δμῳή.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγ’ ἐγὼν ἀναβᾶσ’ ὑπερώϊα σιγαλόεντα
εἴπω σῇ ἀλόχῳ, τῇ τις θεὸς ὕπνον ἐπῶρσε.
sentences.l:
But come, I, having gone up to the glossy upper rooms,
let me tell your wife, on whom some god has sent sleep.”
sentences.i: But come, let me go up to the glossy upper rooms and tell your wife, on whom some god has sent sleep.”
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγ’ with the aorist subjunctive εἴπω is 'come, let me tell'. ἐγών is the epic form of ἐγώ. ἀναβᾶσα is the aorist participle of ἀναβαίνω 'go up', and ὑπερώϊα are the upper rooms of the house, with σιγαλόεντα 'glossy', the house rendering. σῇ ἀλόχῳ is 'to your wife', and τῇ the relative 'on whom'. ἐπῶρσε is the aorist of ἐπόρνυμι 'rouse upon, send on'. The Greek names no god. This ends the speech.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς
sentences.l: Her answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to her:
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph. This line is already published and keeps its English; here Murray prints no stop at the end of it, so the unit ends with the line and the speech begins in the next unit. ἀπαμειβόμενος is 'answering', and πολύμητις 'many-wiled' is the house epithet of Odysseus.

sentences.t: μή πω τήνδ’ ἐπέγειρε·
sentences.l: “Not yet this woman rouse;
sentences.i: “Do not wake her yet;
sentences.n: Odysseus answers. μή πω is 'not yet', with the present imperative ἐπέγειρε (ἐπεγείρω 'wake, rouse'): 'do not go waking her'. τήνδε 'this one' is Penelope, pointed at as if she were in the room. The ano teleia closes a very short unit in mid-line.

sentences.t:
σὺ δ’ ἐνθάδε εἰπὲ γυναιξὶν
ἐλθέμεν, αἵ περ πρόσθεν ἀεικέα μηχανόωντο.
sentences.l:
but you, here tell the women
to come, those who before unseemly things devised.”
sentences.i: but you, tell the women to come here, the very ones who before contrived unseemly things.”
sentences.n: σὺ δέ is 'but you'. ἐνθάδε is 'here' (the suffix -δε again). εἰπέ is the aorist imperative of εἶπον, and ἐλθέμεν the infinitive in -έμεν of ἔρχομαι: what he tells her to tell them. αἵ περ is 'the very ones who', with περ stressing the relative, and πρόσθεν is 'before'. μηχανόωντο is the uncontracted imperfect middle of μηχανάομαι 'contrive', -όωντο for Attic -ῶντο, and ἀεικέα is a neuter plural, 'unseemly things'. This ends the speech.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφη,
sentences.l: So then he spoke,
sentences.i: So he spoke,
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph. ἔφη is a past tense of φημί, 'he said', and ἄρα (ἄρ’) marks the speech as now finished. The speaker is Odysseus.

sentences.t:
γρηῢς δὲ διὲκ μεγάροιο βεβήκει
ἀγγελέουσα γυναιξὶ καὶ ὀτρυνέουσα νέεσθαι.
sentences.l:
and the old woman out through the hall had gone,
to bring word to the women and to urge them to come.
sentences.i: and the old woman went out through the hall to carry the message to the women and to urge them to come.
sentences.n: γρηῢς is 'old woman'. βεβήκει is the pluperfect of βαίνω, 'had gone', and διέκ μεγάροιο is 'out through the hall' (διέκ with the genitive). ἀγγελέουσα and ὀτρυνέουσα are future participles of purpose, 'to bring word' and 'to urge', and νέεσθαι 'to come' is the uncontracted infinitive of νέομαι.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὁ Τηλέμαχον καὶ βουκόλον ἠδὲ συβώτην
εἰς ἓ καλεσσάμενος ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
But he, Telemachus and the cowherd and the swineherd
to himself having called, winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: Then he called Telemachus, the cowherd and the swineherd to him, and spoke winged words:
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὁ is 'but he', Odysseus. ἠδέ is the epic 'and', and the cowherd and the swineherd are named only by their trades. εἰς ἕ is 'to himself', ἕ the reflexive pronoun, and καλεσσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of καλέω with the doubled σ, 'having called to himself'. The last words are the speech formula, 'spoke winged words'. The ano teleia introduces the speech.

sentences.t: ἄρχετε νῦν νέκυας φορέειν καὶ ἄνωχθε γυναῖκας·
sentences.l: “Begin now the corpses to carry, and bid the women;
sentences.i: “Begin now to carry the corpses, and bid the women do the same;
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph. Odysseus speaks, to the three men. ἄρχετε is the plural imperative of ἄρχω 'begin', with the infinitive φορέειν, the uncontracted form of φορεῖν, 'to carry'. ἄνωχθε is the perfect imperative of ἄνωγα 'bid', used as a present, and its object is γυναῖκας; the infinitive 'to carry' is left to be understood, and the infinitive of the next unit hangs on the same word.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα θρόνους περικαλλέας ἠδὲ τραπέζας
ὕδατι καὶ σπόγγοισι πολυτρήτοισι καθαίρειν.
sentences.l:
and then the very fair chairs and the tables
with water and with sponges full-of-holes to cleanse.
sentences.i: and then to clean the very fair chairs and tables with water and with many-holed sponges.
sentences.n: The infinitive καθαίρειν 'to cleanse' hangs on ἄνωχθε. θρόνους are chairs, with περικαλλέας 'very fair' (the περι- is 'very'), and ἠδέ is 'and'. ὕδατι and σπόγγοισι are datives of means, and σπόγγοι are sea-sponges. πολυτρήτοισι is built on πολύς 'many' and τρητός 'bored, pierced': a sponge with many holes. The two lines come back, with the verb in the past, when the women do the work at 452–453.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπὴν δὴ πάντα δόμον κατακοσμήσησθε,
δμῳὰς ἐξαγαγόντες ἐϋσταθέος μεγάροιο,
μεσσηγύς τε θόλου καὶ ἀμύμονος ἕρκεος αὐλῆς,
sentences.l:
But when indeed all the house you have set in order,
the maidservants having led out of the well-standing hall,
between the tholos and the blameless fence of the courtyard,
sentences.i: And when you have set the whole house in order and have led the maids out of the sturdy hall, between the round building and the blameless fence of the courtyard,
sentences.n: The orders go on. ἐπήν with the aorist subjunctive κατακοσμήσησθε is 'when you have set in order'. ἐξαγαγόντες is the aorist participle of ἐξάγω 'lead out', and δμῳάς 'maidservants' its object. ἐϋσταθέος 'well-standing' is built on ἐύ 'well' and the root of ἵστημι 'stand'. μεσσηγύς is 'between', with two genitives. θόλος is a round building with a conical roof; the Greek names it only as one of two landmarks, with the courtyard's fence, and the literal layer keeps the word 'tholos' where the plain one says 'round building'. ἕρκος is the 'fence' of the courtyard, and ἀμύμων 'blameless' the standing epithet, whose real sense is not known. The sentence runs six lines, so the unit is cut at the comma where the syntax pauses most.

sentences.t:
θεινέμεναι ξίφεσιν τανυήκεσιν, εἰς ὅ κε πασέων
ψυχὰς ἐξαφέλησθε καὶ ἐκλελάθωντ’ Ἀφροδίτης,
τὴν ἄρ’ ὑπὸ μνηστῆρσιν ἔχον μίσγοντό τε λάθρη.
sentences.l:
to strike with long-pointed swords, until of all of them
the lives you have taken out, and they have forgotten Aphrodite,
which they were having under the suitors, and mingled in secret.”
sentences.i: strike them with long-pointed swords, until you have taken the lives of every one of them and they have forgotten the Aphrodite they had beneath the suitors, mingling with them in secret.”
sentences.n: θεινέμεναι is the infinitive in -έμεναι of θείνω 'strike', standing as a command that picks up ἄνωχθε. τανυήκης 'long-pointed' is built on τανυ- 'long' and the root of ἀκή 'point'; the exact picture is not certain. εἰς ὅ κε with the aorist subjunctive ἐξαφέλησθε is 'until you have taken out', and ψυχάς here are the 'lives' of living people, the breath that leaves at death. πασέων is the genitive plural of πᾶσα (Attic πασῶν). ἐκλελάθωντ’ is the reduplicated aorist subjunctive of ἐκλανθάνομαι 'forget utterly'. Ἀφροδίτης stands for sexual love itself. τὴν ἄρ’ ὑπὸ μνηστῆρσιν ἔχον is 'which they were having beneath the suitors', with ὑπό and the dative; μίσγοντο is 'they mingled' (μίσγομαι 'mix, have intercourse with'), and λάθρη 'in secret'. This ends the speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, αἱ δὲ γυναῖκες ἀολλέες ἦλθον ἅπασαι,
αἴν’ ὀλοφυρόμεναι, θαλερὸν κατὰ δάκρυ χέουσαι.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and the women all together came, every one,
terribly lamenting, an abundant tear shedding.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the women came all together, every one of them, lamenting terribly and shedding abundant tears.
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph. ὣς ἔφαθ’ is 'so he spoke', with ἔφαθ’ the elided ἔφατο. ἀολλέες is 'gathered together', and ἅπασαι 'every one'. αἴν’ is αἰνά, the adverb 'terribly', from αἰνός 'fearsome'. ὀλοφυρόμεναι is the participle of ὀλοφύρομαι 'lament'. θαλερόν is 'abundant', and δάκρυ 'tear' is a singular used for tears in general. κατά ... χέουσαι is tmesis, the preverb standing apart from its verb, for 'pouring down'.

sentences.t:
πρῶτα μὲν οὖν νέκυας φόρεον κατατεθνηῶτας,
κὰδ δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπ’ αἰθούσῃ τίθεσαν εὐερκέος αὐλῆς,
ἀλλήλοισιν ἐρείδουσαι·
sentences.i: First they carried the corpses, the dead men, and laid them down beneath the portico of the well-secured courtyard, propping them against one another;
sentences.n: πρῶτα μὲν οὖν is 'first then'. φόρεον is the imperfect of φορέω 'carry', and κατατεθνηῶτας the perfect participle of καταθνῄσκω, 'dead', with the lengthened Homeric ending -ηῶτας. κὰδ ... τίθεσαν is tmesis for 'set down': κάδ is κατά with its last letter assimilated before δ. αἴθουσα is the roofed portico, and εὐερκέος 'well-fenced' is εὖ with ἕρκος 'fence', as at 442. ἐρείδουσαι is the participle of ἐρείδω 'prop, press', feminine because the women are the subject.

sentences.t:
σήμαινε δ’ Ὀδυσσεὺς
αὐτὸς ἐπισπέρχων·
sentences.l:
and Odysseus gave the orders
himself, urging them on;
sentences.i: and Odysseus himself gave the orders, hurrying them on;
sentences.n: σήμαινε is the imperfect of σημαίνω 'give a sign', here 'give the orders', as at 427. αὐτός 'himself' puts Odysseus in charge of the work. ἐπισπέρχων is the participle of ἐπισπέρχω 'press on, hurry'.

sentences.t: ταὶ δ’ ἐκφόρεον καὶ ἀνάγκῃ.
sentences.l: and they carried out, even under compulsion.
sentences.i: and they carried them out, under compulsion too.
sentences.n: ταί is the older demonstrative for αἱ, 'they', the women. ἐκφόρεον is the imperfect of ἐκφορέω, the verb of φόρεον with the prefix ἐκ- 'out'. καί here is 'also, even', and ἀνάγκῃ 'by compulsion' is a dative of means: the Greek does not say what compels them, though Odysseus is urging them in the same line.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα θρόνους περικαλλέας ἠδὲ τραπέζας
ὕδατι καὶ σπόγγοισι πολυτρήτοισι κάθαιρον.
sentences.l:
And then the very fair chairs and the tables
with water and with sponges full-of-holes they cleansed.
sentences.i: Then they cleaned the very fair chairs and tables with water and with many-holed sponges.
sentences.n: These two lines carry out Odysseus's order of 438–439 in the same words, the infinitive καθαίρειν there becoming the imperfect κάθαιρον here. The order is obeyed to the letter.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Τηλέμαχος καὶ βουκόλος ἠδὲ συβώτης
λίστροισιν δάπεδον πύκα ποιητοῖο δόμοιο
ξῦον·
sentences.i: While Telemachus, the cowherd and the swineherd scraped the floor of the well-built house with scrapers;
sentences.n: λίστρον is a tool for scraping, a scraper. δάπεδον is 'floor'. ποιητοῖο δόμοιο is 'of the well-built house', ποιητός being 'made, built', with the genitive in -οιο; πύκα 'closely' stands beside ποιητοῖο, 'closely built', though it could also be taken with ξῦον, 'scraped thoroughly'. ξῦον is the imperfect of ξύω 'scrape'.

sentences.t: ταὶ δ’ ἐφόρεον δμῳαί, τίθεσαν δὲ θύραζε.
sentences.l: and the maidservants carried it away, and set it outside.
sentences.i: and the maids carried it away and put it outside.
sentences.n: ταί is 'they', explained by δμῳαί 'the maidservants'. ἐφόρεον 'carried' has no object in the Greek; what they carry off is understood to be what the men scraped up. τίθεσαν is 'set down', and θύραζε 'out of doors' has the suffix -ζε, the same as -δε.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπειδὴ πᾶν μέγαρον διεκοσμήσαντο,
δμῳὰς δ’ ἐξαγαγόντες ἐϋσταθέος μεγάροιο,
μεσσηγύς τε θόλου καὶ ἀμύμονος ἕρκεος αὐλῆς,
εἴλεον ἐν στείνει, ὅθεν οὔ πως ἦεν ἀλύξαι.
sentences.l:
But when the whole hall they had set in order,
and the maidservants having led out of the well-standing hall,
between the tholos and the blameless fence of the courtyard,
they penned them in a narrow place, from where in no way was it possible to escape.
sentences.i: And when they had set the whole hall in order, they led the maids out of the sturdy hall, between the round building and the blameless fence of the courtyard, and penned them in a narrow place from which there was no way to escape.
sentences.n: The first line is 440 in the past, with μέγαρον for δόμον: διεκοσμήσαντο is the aorist middle of διακοσμέω 'put in order', and ἐπειδή 'when' replaces ἐπὴν δή. The next two lines repeat 441–442, so the order is carried out as it was given. εἴλεον is the imperfect of εἱλέω 'shut in, pen', and ἐν στείνει 'in a narrow place' is the dative of στεῖνος 'narrow space'. ὅθεν 'from which' has the place-from suffix -θεν, ἦεν is ἦν 'it was', and ἀλύξαι is the aorist infinitive of ἀλύσκω 'escape'; οὔ πως is 'in no way'.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δὲ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἦρχ’ ἀγορεύειν·
sentences.l: And to them prudent Telemachus began to speak:
sentences.i: Prudent Telemachus began to speak to them:
sentences.n: τοῖσι is 'to them', the penned women. ἦρχε is the imperfect of ἄρχω 'begin', with ἀγορεύειν 'to speak'. The epithet πεπνυμένος 'prudent' keeps its rendering here, though what follows is a cruel decision. The ano teleia introduces the speech.

sentences.t:
μὴ μὲν δὴ καθαρῷ θανάτῳ ἀπὸ θυμὸν ἑλοίμην
τάων, αἳ δὴ ἐμῇ κεφαλῇ κατ’ ὀνείδεα χεῦαν
μητέρι θ’ ἡμετέρῃ παρά τε μνηστῆρσιν ἴαυον.
sentences.l:
“Not at all by a clean death may I take the life from those
who on my head reproaches poured down,
and on our mother, and beside the suitors slept.”
sentences.i: “May I never take the lives of those women by a clean death, women who poured reproaches on my head and on our mother, and who slept beside the suitors.”
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph. Telemachus speaks. μὴ μὲν δή with the optative ἑλοίμην is a wish or vow with a negative, 'may I never'. The thought is that they will not have the clean death of the sword. The tmesis ἀπὸ ... ἑλοίμην is 'take away', and θυμός here is the life, the heart that leaves at death. ἐμῇ κεφαλῇ is 'on my head', the head standing for the person; κατ’ ... χεῦαν is tmesis for the aorist of καταχέω, 'poured down upon', with ὀνείδεα 'reproaches'. ἡμετέρῃ is 'our': the plural may take in Odysseus, who stands listening, or stand for 'my' alone, and the Greek does not say which. ἴαυον is the imperfect of ἰαύω 'lie, sleep', and παρά with the dative is 'beside'. This ends the speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφη, καὶ πεῖσμα νεὸς κυανοπρῴροιο
κίονος ἐξάψας μεγάλης περίβαλλε θόλοιο,
ὑψόσ’ ἐπεντανύσας, μή τις ποσὶν οὖδας ἵκοιτο.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and a cable of a dark-prowed ship
to a great pillar having fastened he threw it round the tholos,
stretching it high, that none with her feet the ground might reach.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and tying the cable of a dark-prowed ship to a great pillar he threw it around the round building, stretching it high up so that none of them could touch the ground with their feet.
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph. ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφη closes the speech: 'so he spoke'. πεῖσμα is the 'cable' that holds a ship, and νεός the genitive of ναῦς; κυανοπρῴροιο 'dark-prowed' is the house epithet. ἐξάψας is the aorist participle of ἐξάπτω 'tie from', governing κίονος μεγάλης 'a great pillar' in the genitive, and περίβαλλε is the imperfect 'threw round'. θόλοιο is the round building again. ἐπεντανύσας is 'stretching it taut', and ὑψόσ’ 'high up'. μή τις ... ἵκοιτο is a negative purpose clause with the optative: τις 'any one', and ποσίν 'with her feet'.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἂν ἢ κίχλαι τανυσίπτεροι ἠὲ πέλειαι
ἕρκει ἐνιπλήξωσι, τό θ’ ἑστήκῃ ἐνὶ θάμνῳ,
αὖλιν ἐσιέμεναι, στυγερὸς δ’ ὑπεδέξατο κοῖτος,
sentences.l:
And as when either thrushes, long-winged, or doves
strike into a snare, which is set in a thicket,
to enter their roost, and a hateful resting-place receives them,
sentences.i: As when long-winged thrushes or doves strike a snare that is set in a thicket, as they hurry to enter their roost, and a hateful resting-place receives them,
sentences.n: ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἂν opens a simile, 'as when', with ἄν and the aorist subjunctive ἐνιπλήξωσι (ἐμπλήσσω 'strike into'), a general picture. κίχλαι are thrushes and πέλειαι doves, the species of both being unknown; τανυσίπτερος 'long-winged' is τανυ- 'long' with πτερόν 'wing'. ἕρκος, 'fence' elsewhere in this part, is here a snare or net; τό is the relative 'which', and ἑστήκῃ the perfect subjunctive of ἵστημι, 'stands, is set up'. ἐσιέμεναι is the infinitive of ἐσίημι, in -μεναι, of purpose, and αὖλις is a place to pass the night. στυγερός is 'hateful' and κοῖτος 'resting-place': the snare takes the place of the roost. ὑπεδέξατο is the aorist of ὑποδέχομαι 'receive'. The simile is cut at the comma because the whole sentence runs five lines.

sentences.t:
ὣς αἵ γ’ ἑξείης κεφαλὰς ἔχον, ἀμφὶ δὲ πάσαις
δειρῇσι βρόχοι ἦσαν, ὅπως οἴκτιστα θάνοιεν.
sentences.l:
so these in a row held their heads, and around all
their necks were nooses, that most pitiably they might die.
sentences.i: so these held their heads in a row, and around the necks of all of them were nooses, so that they would die in the most pitiable way.
sentences.n: ὣς αἵ γε answers the simile: 'so these women'. ἑξείης is 'in a row'. κεφαλὰς ἔχον is the imperfect 'held their heads'. ἀμφὶ δὲ πάσαις δειρῇσι is 'and around the necks of all', ἀμφί standing apart from its noun, with δειρῇσι the dative plural in -ῃσι of δειρή 'neck'. βρόχος is 'noose', and ἦσαν 'were'. ὅπως with the optative θάνοιεν is 'so that they might die', and οἴκτιστα is the superlative adverb of οἰκτρός 'pitiable': it is what the hanging is meant to bring about.

sentences.t: ἤσπαιρον δὲ πόδεσσι μίνυνθά περ οὔ τι μάλα δήν.
sentences.l: And they twitched with their feet for a little while, yet not at all very long.
sentences.i: Their feet twitched for a little while, but not for very long.
sentences.n: ἤσπαιρον is the imperfect of ἀσπαίρω 'quiver, twitch', the movement of a dying body. πόδεσσι is a dative plural in -εσσι. μίνυνθα is 'for a little while', with περ 'though'; οὔ τι μάλα δήν is 'not at all very long', δήν meaning 'for a long time'. The line states the death without comment.

sentences.t: ἐκ δὲ Μελάνθιον ἦγον ἀνὰ πρόθυρόν τε καὶ αὐλήν·
sentences.l: And out Melanthius they led through the forecourt and the courtyard;
sentences.i: Then they led Melanthius out through the forecourt and the courtyard;
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph, passing from the women to Melanthius, who is named here without a word of introduction. ἐκ ... ἦγον is tmesis, 'led out'. ἀνά with the accusative is 'up through, along'. πρόθυρον is the forecourt, the space before the door, and αὐλή the courtyard. The subject of ἦγον is not named.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δ’ ἀπὸ μὲν ῥῖνάς τε καὶ οὔατα νηλέϊ χαλκῷ
τάμνον, μήδεά τ’ ἐξέρυσαν, κυσὶν ὠμὰ δάσασθαι,
χεῖράς τ’ ἠδὲ πόδας κόπτον κεκοτηότι θυμῷ.
sentences.l:
And from him off the nose and the ears with pitiless bronze
they cut, and tore out his genitals, raw for the dogs to share,
and hands and feet they chopped with a grudge-bearing heart.
sentences.i: They cut off his nose and ears with the pitiless bronze, tore out his genitals for the dogs to eat raw, and chopped off his hands and feet with a heart full of resentment.
sentences.n: τοῦ is 'from him', and ἀπὸ ... τάμνον is tmesis for 'cut off' (τάμνω is the Ionic form of τέμνω). ῥῖνας is the plural of ῥίς 'nose', a plural that stands for the nose as a whole; οὔατα is 'ears' (Attic ὦτα). νηλέϊ 'pitiless' is the house rendering, and χαλκῷ 'bronze' stands for the sword. μήδεα here is 'genitals', a different word from μήδεα 'counsels'. ἐξέρυσαν is the aorist of ἐξερύω 'draw out'. κυσὶν ὠμὰ δάσασθαι is 'raw things for dogs to share out', δάσασθαι being the aorist middle infinitive of δατέομαι 'divide among themselves'. κόπτον is the imperfect 'chopped'. κεκοτηότι θυμῷ 'with a grudge-bearing heart' is the perfect participle of κοτέω 'bear a grudge', from κότος 'resentment'. The Greek reports it without comment.

sentences.t:
οἱ μὲν ἔπειτ’ ἀπονιψάμενοι χεῖράς τε πόδας τε
εἰς Ὀδυσῆα δόμονδε κίον, τετέλεστο δὲ ἔργον·
sentences.l:
They then, having washed off hands and feet,
to Odysseus to the house went, and the work was finished;
sentences.i: Then they washed their hands and feet and went into the house to Odysseus, and the work was done;
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph. οἱ μὲν ἔπειτα is 'they then'. ἀπονιψάμενοι is the aorist middle participle of ἀπονίζω 'wash off', the middle meaning 'wash one's own'; χεῖράς τε πόδας τε is 'hands and feet'. δόμονδε 'to the house' has the direction suffix -δε. κίον is the imperfect of κίω 'go'. τετέλεστο is the pluperfect passive of τελέω 'finish', 'had been finished', and ἔργον 'work' is the word for the 'deed' that the nurse saw at 408.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ὅ γε προσέειπε φίλην τροφὸν Εὐρύκλειαν·
sentences.l: but he addressed the dear nurse Eurycleia:
sentences.i: Then he spoke to his dear nurse Eurycleia:
sentences.n: ὅ γε is 'he' with emphasis: Odysseus, who now speaks to the nurse with the others back. προσέειπε is 'addressed'. φίλην τροφὸν Εὐρύκλειαν is the same standing phrase as at 419, here in the accusative as the person addressed.

sentences.t:
οἶσε θέειον, γρηΰ, κακῶν ἄκος, οἶσε δέ μοι πῦρ,
ὄφρα θεειώσω μέγαρον·
sentences.l:
“Bring sulphur, old woman, the remedy of evils, and bring me fire,
so that I may purify the hall with sulphur;
sentences.i: “Bring sulphur, old woman, the cure for ills, and bring me fire, so that I may purify the hall with sulphur;
sentences.n: Odysseus speaks again. οἶσε is the aorist imperative of φέρω 'bring', and it is said twice. θέειον is 'sulphur' (Attic θεῖον), the same word as θήϊον at 493: sulphur was burned to cleanse a place. κακῶν ἄκος 'remedy of evils' stands in apposition. ὄφρα with the aorist subjunctive θεειώσω, from θεειόω 'treat with sulphur', is 'so that I may purify with sulphur'.

sentences.t:
σὺ δὲ Πηνελόπειαν
ἐλθεῖν ἐνθάδ’ ἄνωχθι σὺν ἀμφιπόλοισι γυναιξί·
sentences.l:
and you, Penelope
to come here bid, with her attendant women;
sentences.i: and you, bid Penelope come here with her attendant women;
sentences.n: σὺ δέ is 'and you', handing the next task to the nurse. ἐλθεῖν is the aorist infinitive of ἔρχομαι, and ἄνωχθι the imperative of ἄνωγα 'bid', in the form with -θι. ἀμφίπολοι are 'attendants', so ἀμφιπόλοισι γυναιξί is 'attendant women', and σύν with the dative is 'with'.

sentences.t: πάσας δ’ ὄτρυνον δμῳὰς κατὰ δῶμα νέεσθαι.
sentences.l: and all the maidservants urge to come through the house.”
sentences.i: and urge all the maidservants to come through the house.”
sentences.n: ὄτρυνον is the aorist imperative of ὀτρύνω 'urge', and πάσας δμῳάς 'all the maidservants' its object. κατὰ δῶμα is 'through the house', and νέεσθαι the infinitive 'to come'. This ends the speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε φίλη τροφὸς Εὐρύκλεια·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed the dear nurse Eurycleia:
sentences.i: Then his dear nurse Eurycleia spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: This line is already published, and keeps its English. It is the same reply formula as at 419, with the nurse again as speaker.

sentences.t: ναὶ δὴ ταῦτά γε, τέκνον ἐμόν, κατὰ μοῖραν ἔειπες.
sentences.l: “Yes indeed, these things, my child, according to what is fitting you have said.
sentences.i: “Yes indeed, my child, you have spoken as is fitting.
sentences.n: Eurycleia answers. ναὶ δή is 'yes indeed', and ταῦτά γε 'these things at least'. τέκνον ἐμόν is 'my child', with the possessive after the noun. κατὰ μοῖραν is 'according to what is fitting', μοῖρα being 'portion, due'. ἔειπες is the aorist of εἶπον with its doubled vowel (Attic εἶπες).

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε τοι χλαῖνάν τε χιτῶνά τε εἵματ’ ἐνείκω,
μηδ’ οὕτω ῥάκεσιν πεπυκασμένος εὐρέας ὤμους
ἕσταθ’ ἐνὶ μεγάροισι·
sentences.i: But come, let me bring you a cloak and a tunic for clothing, and do not stand like this in the halls with your broad shoulders wrapped in rags;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε with the aorist subjunctive ἐνείκω (ἐνέγκω) is 'but come, let me bring'; τοι is σοι 'for you'. χλαῖνα is 'cloak' and χιτών 'tunic', with εἵματ’ 'clothes' as the general word beside them. μηδ’ οὕτω is 'and not thus', with the perfect imperative ἕσταθι (ἕσταθ’ elided) 'stand'. πεπυκασμένος is the perfect passive participle of πυκάζω 'cover closely', with ῥάκεσιν 'rags' as the means, and εὐρέας ὤμους 'broad shoulders' is an accusative of respect. The ano teleia closes the unit in mid-line.

sentences.t: νεμεσσητὸν δέ κεν εἴη.
sentences.l: and a thing to resent it would be.”
sentences.i: for that would be a cause for resentment.”
sentences.n: νεμεσσητόν is a verbal adjective of νεμεσάω 'feel righteous resentment': 'deserving resentment'. κε(ν) with the optative εἴη is 'would be', the potential. The Greek gives only the verdict, not who would resent it. This ends the speech.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: Her answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to her:
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph. This line is already published, and keeps its English. It is the same reply-formula as at 430: ἀπαμειβόμενος is 'answering', and πολύμητις 'many-wiled' is the house epithet of Odysseus.

sentences.t: πῦρ νῦν μοι πρώτιστον ἐνὶ μεγάροισι γενέσθω.
sentences.l: “Fire now for me first of all in the halls let there be.”
sentences.i: “Let there be fire for me now in the halls, first of all.”
sentences.n: Odysseus answers. πῦρ stands first for emphasis. He takes up the fire he asked for and puts it before the clothes the nurse has offered. πρώτιστον is the superlative of πρῶτος used as an adverb, 'first of all'. μοι is 'for me', and γενέσθω the aorist imperative of γίγνομαι, 'let it come to be'. This ends the speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε φίλη τροφὸς Εὐρύκλεια,
ἤνεικεν δ’ ἄρα πῦρ καὶ θήϊον·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, nor did the dear nurse Eurycleia disobey,
and she brought fire and sulphur;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and his dear nurse Eurycleia did not disobey; she brought fire and sulphur;
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph. ὣς ἔφατ’ is 'so he spoke', ἔφατ’ the elided ἔφατο. ἀπίθησε is the aorist of ἀπιθέω 'disobey', and οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε 'did not disobey' means she obeyed. ἤνεικεν is a past tense of φέρω (Attic ἤνεγκεν), and θήϊον is the epic spelling of θεῖον 'sulphur'. The ano teleia closes the unit in mid-line.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ὀδυσσεὺς
εὖ διεθείωσεν μέγαρον καὶ δῶμα καὶ αὐλήν.
sentences.l:
and Odysseus
thoroughly purified with sulphur the hall and the house and the courtyard.
sentences.i: and Odysseus thoroughly purified the hall, the house and the courtyard with the sulphur.
sentences.n: διεθείωσεν is the aorist of διαθειόω 'purify thoroughly with sulphur', the verb of θεειώσω with the prefix δια- 'throughout'; the augment stands between prefix and stem. εὖ is 'well, thoroughly'. μέγαρον καὶ δῶμα καὶ αὐλήν runs outward in three words: the hall, the house, the courtyard.

sentences.t:
γρηῢς δ’ αὖτ’ ἀπέβη διὰ δώματα κάλ’ Ὀδυσῆος
ἀγγελέουσα γυναιξὶ καὶ ὀτρυνέουσα νέεσθαι·
sentences.l:
And the old woman in turn went away through the fair house of Odysseus,
to bring word to the women and to urge them to come;
sentences.i: The old woman, for her part, went away through the fair house of Odysseus to carry the message to the women and to urge them to come;
sentences.n: The second line is a line already published, and keeps its English. γρηῢς is 'old woman', and αὖτε 'in turn, for her part'. ἀπέβη is the aorist of ἀποβαίνω 'go away'. δώματα is a plural that stands for the one house, and κάλ’ is the elided καλά 'fair'. ἀγγελέουσα and ὀτρυνέουσα are future participles of purpose. The ano teleia closes the unit before the women come in.

sentences.t:
αἱ δ’ ἴσαν ἐκ μεγάροιο δάος μετὰ χερσὶν ἔχουσαι.
αἱ μὲν ἄρ’ ἀμφεχέοντο καὶ ἠσπάζοντ’ Ὀδυσῆα,
καὶ κύνεον ἀγαπαζόμεναι κεφαλήν τε καὶ ὤμους
χεῖράς τ’ αἰνύμεναι·
sentences.l:
And they went out of the hall, torches in their hands holding,
and they poured themselves about him and greeted Odysseus,
and kissed him, gladly welcoming, both head and shoulders,
and clasping his hands;
sentences.i: And they went out of the hall, holding torches in their hands, and flung themselves round Odysseus and greeted him, and welcomed him gladly, kissing his head and shoulders, and clasping his hands;
sentences.n: The first and third lines are lines already published, and keep their English. ἴσαν is the imperfect of εἶμι 'go', and δάος 'torch' is the epic word. ἀμφεχέοντο is the imperfect of ἀμφιχέομαι 'pour oneself round', that is embrace, and ἠσπάζοντο the imperfect of ἀσπάζομαι 'greet'. κύνεον is 'kissed', and ἀγαπαζόμεναι 'welcoming gladly'; κεφαλήν τε καὶ ὤμους 'head and shoulders' are accusatives of the part kissed. αἰνύμεναι is the participle of αἴνυμαι 'take hold of', so χεῖράς τ’ αἰνύμεναι is 'clasping his hands'. The ano teleia closes the unit in mid-line.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ γλυκὺς ἵμερος ᾕρει
κλαυθμοῦ καὶ στοναχῆς, γίγνωσκε δ’ ἄρα φρεσὶ πάσας.
sentences.l:
and him sweet longing seized
for weeping and groaning, and he knew in his mind them all.
sentences.i: and a sweet longing for weeping and groaning came over him, and in his mind he recognised every one of them.
sentences.n: τὸν is 'him'. γλυκὺς ἵμερος is 'sweet longing, desire', with the genitive κλαυθμοῦ καὶ στοναχῆς 'for weeping and groaning'. ᾕρει is the imperfect of αἱρέω 'seize'. γίγνωσκε is the imperfect of γιγνώσκω, 'was recognising', and φρεσί is the dative plural of φρήν, 'in his mind'; πάσας 'all of them' are the women. The Greek gives only what he feels and knows as the women embrace him, and the part ends there.
